hints: Imagine you are building rising picks and keeping, for each possible length, the smallest last value you have seen. Why would a smaller last value be better?

Patience-sorting idea: keep an array tails where tails[k] is the smallest possible last value of a rising pick of length k+1. For each number, binary search the first tail ≥ it and replace it (or append).

1. tails = empty, size = 0.
  2. For each x: binary search the first index with tails[idx] ≥ x.
  3. Set tails[idx] = x; if idx == size, size++.
  4. Return size.

approaches.name: Brute force
approaches.idea: Try every subsequence and check if it is strictly rising.

approaches.name: Better
approaches.idea: DP: len[i] = 1 + max len[j] for j < i with nums[j] < nums[i].

approaches.name: Optimal
approaches.idea: Keep smallest tails per length and binary search for each element.

explain: For [4,10,4,3,8,9]: tails goes [4] → [4,10] → [4,10] (4 replaces 4) → [3,10] → [3,8] → [3,8,9]. Size 3 is the answer. A smaller tail for the same length can only make it easier to extend later, so replacing is safe. Note tails is not itself a real pick — only its size matters. Using 'first tail ≥ x' (not >) keeps it strictly rising, so [6,6,6] gives 1.
recognize: Longest subsequence (keep order, skip allowed) that strictly increases → LIS: O(n²) DP or tails + binary search.
